newsitem.title: FRANCE: Japan's Nissan sees modest car sales growth.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Nissan sees modest car sales growth.

text.p: Japan's Nissan Motor Co Ltd said on Tuesday it expected modest sales growth in car markets around the world although Europe looks stronger than most.

In a speech at the Paris Car Show to launch the new Primera, Nissan President Yoshikazu Hanawa said global growth in car sales should reach 3.5 per cent his year, up from less than one per cent in 1995.
"The combined tri-polar markets of Japan, the U.S. and Europe recorded almost no increase in 1995 but should rise by 2.4 per cent this year," Hanawa said.
European sales should grow around by five per cent this year to 13.9 million.

"It is an indication that a steady recovery is underway. One reason for this modest growth perhaps stems from the difficulties or reluctance faced by European member states to introduce economic stimuli due to planned monetary union in 1999," Hanawa said.
Analysts say Europe's growth, where forecasts settle at between four and six percent for 1996, may look healthy on the surface.
But the sales figures mask two negatives - sales of stocks which could not be sold last year at knock-down prices, and sales resulting from government incentives to junk old, polluting cars.
The underlying rate of growth in Europe is said to be closer to two percent than five or six percent, these analysts say.
Hanawa said the company's mid to long-term strategy called for Nissan's global production to be raised to three million cars a year from 2.7 million currently.

"Of this, some 1.8 million will be manufactured at Nissan's domestic plants and the remainder offshore. This global manufacturing balance is intended to maximise the benefits of local supply, and limit the dangers of exhange rate fluctuations.....," Hanawa said.

The Nissan Primera, a large family car, will be launched on all European markets in the next six months. As well as entrenched competition from companies like Renault and Peugeot of France with their Laguna and 406, and the General Motors Corp subsidiary's Opel Vectra, the Paris car sees the debut of more powerful opposition in this sector.
German mass car maker Volkswagen launches the all-new Passat, while Ford unveils its face-lifted Mondeo range.

The Primera has received positive coverage by Europe's motoring writers who agree that the car is solidly built and drives well. But they also say the car's styling is bland, and almost identical to the model it replaces.
Hanawa said Nissan plans to sell 130,000 Primeras annually.

In his speech on the Nissan stand Hanawa said the Primera will be offered with a Continuously Variable Transmission by 2000. This type of automatic transmission uses steel belts and offers an infinite amount of gears, the theory being that the technology will always select the exact ratio required for each driving phase.
Hanawa also announced the company will make a Primera Wagon, starting in 1998. Some 20,000 Wagons will be made at the company's plant in Britain.
Nissan also announced it will buy 10,000 1.5 litre diesel engines annually from Peugeot to power its little Micra.
